title: The Real Cost of Growth Capital: Why the Easiest Money Isn't the Cheapest
linkedin:
Redraw on the house. The business credit card. An overdraft that quietly stopped clearing between busy periods.

None of these feel like a financing decision, because no one sits across a desk and assesses an application before the money gets used.

But every one of them has a real cost, even when it never shows up as a clean interest line on the P&L.

Redraw ties a business outcome to the family home. An overdraft that rolls month to month usually carries one of the higher effective rates a business will pay for capital, precisely because it was never structured as long-term funding. A director's loan account feels free, but it still carries an opportunity cost.

Equity sits at the other end and is the easiest to misjudge. No interest, no repayment schedule, so it feels like the cheapest option in the room. It rarely is. Every dollar of equity costs a permanent share of profit for as long as the business exists.

The useful question is never which capital is fastest to access. It is what the specific use of funds actually justifies paying for. A short, self-funding purchase can carry a higher rate. A multi-year growth bet is often where sharing equity, priced properly, turns out cheaper than debt that strangles cash before the upside shows up.

Most owners have never laid the real options side by side. Nobody asked them to slow down long enough to run the comparison before drawing on whatever cash sat closest to hand.

Turns out the easiest money to access is rarely the cheapest. Redraw ties the family home to a business outcome most people would not choose if it were spelled out plainly. A pattern we see often with East Coast business owners: when it is time to fund a new hire, a piece of equipment or a bigger stock order, the decision usually comes down to whatever cash is easiest to reach. Redraw on the mortgage. The business credit card. An overdraft that has quietly stopped clearing between busy periods.

The trouble is that easy access and low cost are not the same thing. Redraw ties a personal asset to a business decision. A permanent overdraft usually carries one of the higher rates a business ends up paying for capital. And equity, which feels free because there is no interest or repayment schedule, actually costs a permanent share of profit for as long as the business exists.

The businesses that fund growth well are not the ones with access to the most capital. They are the ones who take the time to match the cost of the capital to what it is actually funding, a quick, self-funding purchase versus a slower, multi-year growth bet.

If you have never laid your own funding options side by side and compared what each one really costs, it is worth doing before the next big spending decision, not after. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
